analysis.one_liner: Overhauls offshore drilling safety and royalties after the BP spill, splits up the Minerals Management Service, and locks in permanent conservation funding.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 209–193 on July 30, 2010, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the Deepwater Horizon disaster, this bill would break the Interior Department's Minerals Management Service into separate bureaus so the office collecting oil royalties is no longer the same office selling drilling leases. It would require worst-case blowout plans and engineer-certified safety equipment before drilling, lift the cap on what oil companies owe after a spill, end outdated royalty-free leases, protect offshore workers who report safety problems, and permanently dedicate oil revenue to parks and ocean restoration. The House passed it, but the Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers get a fairer return on oil and gas taken from public waters and land, coastal communities get stronger spill response and a Gulf restoration program, offshore workers get whistleblower protection, and park visitors and conservation projects get guaranteed funding of $900 million a year.

how_it_helps.text: Abolishes the Minerals Management Service and splits it into a Bureau of Energy and Resource Management (leasing), a Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (safety inspections), and an Office of Natural Resources Revenue (royalty collection), ending the structure in which one agency both sold leases and policed them.

Requires drilling permit applicants to submit a worst-case blowout scenario with a complete response plan, prove they can handle a worst-case spill, and have their blowout preventers and well designs certified by an independent third party; CEOs must personally certify spill readiness, with civil penalties for false certification.

Repeals the cap on oil spill liability under the Oil Pollution Act and raises required financial responsibility for offshore facilities to $300 million, so taxpayers and coastal residents are less likely to absorb spill costs.
Requires companies holding royalty-free Gulf of Mexico leases to renegotiate them so royalties are owed once prices pass set thresholds, and repeals royalty relief for deepwater Gulf production.

Permanently directs $900 million a year of offshore oil revenue to the Land and Water Conservation Fund and $150 million to the Historic Preservation Fund, without needing annual votes, plus 10 percent to a new ocean and Great Lakes conservation fund.
Creates the first whistleblower protection law for offshore oil and gas workers, barring employers from retaliating against workers who report safety violations.
Requires annual ethics certification for Interior employees who deal with leaseholders and bars former Interior officials for two years from working on matters they handled in office.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies pay through new safety certification requirements, monthly inspections, higher penalties, a $2-per-barrel conservation fee, unlimited spill liability, and renegotiated leases; some of those costs could reach consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The bill shields certain drilling permit applicants from the July 12, 2010 drilling moratorium and bars federal agencies from suspending permit work for activities caught in it, which critics could read as limiting the government's ability to halt drilling pending safety reviews.

The compliance load is heavy: exploration plan review stretches from 30 to 90 days, every facility must be inspected at least monthly, and operators must pay for independent third-party certification, costs that fall first on drillers but can be passed to consumers.
It bans offshore aquaculture outright, declaring any permit for it invalid, foreclosing an ocean food-farming industry rather than regulating it.
Extending spill liability to anyone with more than a 25 percent ownership stake in a responsible party could make investors and joint-venture partners warier of offshore projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is real: safer drilling and a fairer return on public resources, paid for by higher compliance and liability costs in an industry whose failures had just cost taxpayers and the Gulf coast billions. The moratorium-limitation section is the weakest part, easing pressure on permit applicants mid-crisis. On balance the public gains more than it gives up, especially since the biggest costs fall on companies profiting from public waters.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 209–193, the Senate received it, read it twice, and put it on its calendar — and never voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in September 2009, heard three times in the Natural Resources Committee, and ordered reported on a 27–21 committee vote in July 2010 as work accelerated after the April 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout.
On the floor on July 30, 2010, a Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions to end offshore drilling moratoria failed 166–239.
Final House passage was 209–193: 207 of 255 voting Democrats in favor and 2 of 178 Republicans, with 39 Democrats joining nearly all Republicans against.

The Senate received the bill on August 3, 2010, read it twice, placed it on the calendar under General Orders on August 4, and took no further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies came out ahead: they avoided higher safety certification costs, unlimited spill liability, a $2-per-barrel fee, mandatory renegotiation of royalty-free leases, and the restructured agency that would have policed them. The Interior Department also kept its pre-reform structure for another two years.

for.name: Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, guided it through three hearings and a 27–21 committee vote, and managed it on the House floor.

for.name: 207 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Provided nearly all the votes for passage, 207–39.

against.name: 154 of 178 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, 154–2, and against the Democratic procedural structure for the bill.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was received in August 2010 and placed on the calendar.

against.name: Doc Hastings
against.role: Ranking Member, House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Raised a successful point of order against the committee report on the floor, forced recorded votes on amendments, and moved repeatedly to slow the bill's consideration.

against.name: John Cassidy
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to end offshore drilling moratoria; the motion failed 166–239.

against.name: 39 of 253 House Democrats
against.role: House Democrats from energy-producing districts and others

against.name: American Petroleum Institute and offshore drilling interests
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill's liability, fee, and permitting provisions as a post-spill overreaction that would curtail domestic drilling.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party — 207 of 255 voting Democrats for, 2 of 178 Republicans for — though 39 Democrats crossed over against and the two chambers' fates depended on which party controlled them.

industries.note: The bill imposes certified safety equipment, worst-case blowout planning, monthly inspections, unlimited spill liability, a $2-per-barrel fee, and renegotiation of royalty-free leases. Its gain for the public — safer drilling and a fairer return on public resources — comes directly out of industry margins.

industries.industry: Independent safety certifiers and oil spill response firms
industries.note: Mandatory third-party certification of blowout preventers and well designs, and requirements for demonstrated worst-case spill response capability, create paid demand for these services.

industries.industry: Offshore wind and renewable energy developers
industries.note: The bill protects the ocean renewable leasing and licensing process from delay and clarifies competitive and noncompetitive renewable leasing on the Outer Continental Shelf.

industries.industry: Gulf coast fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: A Gulf of Mexico restoration program, restoration account, and higher spill penalties serve communities whose livelihoods depend on a healthy Gulf after the Deepwater Horizon spill.

The bill forbids any federal authority from permitting offshore fish farming and declares existing permits invalid, shutting the industry out rather than regulating it; its interest runs against environmental groups favoring the ban.
